meta.title: Who really said "A woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Verified: Virginia Woolf wrote it in chapter 1 of A Room of One's Own (1929). The book grew from talks she gave at Cambridge in October 1928.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Woolf, word for word: chapter 1 of A Room of One's Own (1929), offered as her 'opinion upon one minor point.'

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From chapter 1 of A Room of One’s Own (1929), word for word. Woolf offers it as “an opinion upon one minor point” near the start of the lecture. The same sentence appears in both 1929 first editions, from the Hogarth Press in London and Harcourt Brace in New York.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Papers read at Newnham and Girton colleges, Cambridge, 20 and 26 October 1928

source.excerpt: All I could do was to offer you an opinion upon one minor point—a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction; and that, as you will see, leaves the great problem of the true nature of woman and the true nature of fiction unsolved.
trail: The sentence appears word for word in chapter 1 of the 1929 Hogarth Press first edition ↗, and identically in the 1929 Harcourt Brace American edition ↗.
Wikiquote lists it in its sourced quotations under A Room of One’s Own (1929), chapter 1, on its Virginia Woolf page ↗. Quote Investigator has no article on the line.
The book grew out of two papers Woolf read on 20 and 26 October 1928 to student societies at Newnham College and Girton College, Cambridge (Wikipedia ↗).

In the last chapter Woolf restates the idea in different words: “it is necessary to have five hundred a year and a room with a lock on the door if you are to write fiction or poetry” (full text, Project Gutenberg Australia ↗).
source.excerptNote: In the original the line is a clause after a dash, not a stand-alone sentence. Woolf frames it modestly as her “opinion upon one minor point.”

source.rightsNote: A Room of One’s Own was first published in 1929, before 1931, so it is in the public domain in the United States. Wikisource’s license notice says the edition was published before 1 January 1931, and Wikipedia ↗ notes that it entered the US public domain on 1 January 2025.

author.name: Virginia Woolf
author.heading: About Virginia Woolf
author.bio: Born Adeline Virginia Stephen, Woolf was a central figure of literary modernism and wrote Mrs Dalloway, To the Lighthouse and Orlando. With her husband Leonard she ran the Hogarth Press, which first published A Room of One’s Own in 1929. The book grew out of two papers she read to women students at Newnham and Girton colleges, Cambridge, in October 1928.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Woolf was asked to speak on “women and fiction.” She told her Cambridge audience she could not give them “a nugget of pure truth.” She offered this practical point instead and spent the rest of the book showing how she reached it. Her argument is that women’s writing had been held back by a lack of money, privacy and leisure, not by a lack of talent.

A few lines later she warns that her “‘I’ is only a convenient term for somebody who has no real being” and tells listeners to “call me Mary Beton, Mary Seton, Mary Carmichael or by any name you please.” The famous sentence itself, though, comes in her opening framing, before that persona takes over.
detailsBody: The “money” becomes specific later in the book: “five hundred a year.” In the closing chapter she writes that “five hundred a year stands for the power to contemplate, that a lock on the door means the power to think for oneself.”
